source.title: Causal Routing for Unlearning
source.authors: Bardh Prenkaj; Andrea D'Angelo; Davide Mottin; Federico Fontana; Davide Gabrielli; Paola Velardi; Stefano Faralli

record.tranche_reason: The paper uses neuron localization and gating as a tool for machine unlearning, but does not test whether neurons have one or a small number of human-interpretable jobs, nor whether neuron-based attribution graphs explain behavior.
record.gate_note: The study selects high-variance neurons and gates them for unlearning. Its gate statistics and unlearning outcomes concern this intervention, not the accuracy or completeness of neuron explanations, so the rows are linked to none of the claim versions. Its random-neuron comparison is described as performing worse and close to the original model across models, but the exact model-specific values are not stated in text.
record.test_reason: The study uses variance-selected neurons as gating targets for machine unlearning and reports only its own method's unlearning performance against baselines. It never explains neurons, audits how many have one job, scores explanations by simulation, or builds attribution graphs, so no version of the claim is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors present CRU as a lightweight unlearning method: variance-ranked neurons in the last blocks are gated per token by small trained routers on a frozen base. They also argue that concepts can be reached via the neurons that express them and that suppression should be decided per query. They claim CRU removes knowledge rather than hiding it (0.052 adversarial recall vs 0.250) at far lower memory cost (14 vs 71 GiB).
record.recipe_differences: The study trains input-conditional routing modules to gate high-variance neuron activations for unlearning; it does not use the original study's neuron explanation and held-out activation evaluation procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported outcomes vary with model, benchmark, forget-set size, selected percentile, router settings, and the number and position of gated blocks. The paper reports a non-monotonic percentile effect, including different results at p = 90 and p = 99.

fits_no_version.finding: Gating variance-selected late-layer neurons per token sharply reduces target-knowledge recall (RWKU mean 0.532 to 0.048). Random neurons of the same number in the same layers leave forgetting near the original model.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Concept-related knowledge can be suppressed by input-conditional gating of a small set of variance-selected neurons. This says nothing about whether those neurons have single human-interpretable jobs.

fits_no_version.finding: Forget-set and retain-set variance selections overlap 27–59% across models (Spearman 0.18–0.46). Neuron selection is thus only partly concept-specific.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: High-variance neuron sets selected for a concept are partly concept-specific and partly generically variable.

record.problems: Neuron selection uses activation variance as a stand-in for attribution; the paper reports that a minority of selected neurons are generically variable. The authors state that their loss-shape ablation remains future work. The study does not evaluate explanation accuracy or generalize neuron-interpretablity shares.
record.rows_left_out: Other CRU utility, runtime, memory, percentile, block-position, and neuron-overlap results were left out because they assess unlearning performance or implementation choices rather than the claim's neuron-interpretability versions. The text also reports random neuron selection as performing worse and close to the original model, but exact model-specific values are not stated in text.

record.verdict_notes: T4 tool use. The neuron-overlap result (§D.3.1) and the random-selection ablation concern localization for unlearning, not neuron interpretability, and are correctly left out as claim rows. The paper even notes that a sizable minority of selected neurons are generic rather than concept-specific. That is a statement about its selection method, not about explanation shares.

versions.untested_parts: The Qwen3-32B audit shares, including the proportions of poles with one job, two related jobs, or not-yet-understood jobs.
Interpretability shares across models, dense and mixture-of-experts architectures, or trillion-parameter models.
The InceptionV1 cat-and-car example, pose as a shared feature, and recursive generalization versus superposition.
Whether architecture, regularization, or tools explain messy neurons, and the proposed InceptionV1-sized model estimates.
The study does not build attribution graphs or test whether they explain behavior without a replacement model or reconstruction error.
It does not test neuron explanations against activations beyond the examples used to write them.
It does not score neuron explanations by simulating activations on new text.

source_check.notes: No version bears on this study and no verdicts are needed. The text's 0.532 'original model' baseline equals GD's mean in Figure 5 (Appendix D.2 gives 0.484 for the original model, but only on 3 held-out tuning targets), so treat 0.532 with caution. Figure 3 per-model gate means are 0.01–0.04 forget and 0.82–0.83 retain; the wider 0.01–0.06 and 0.79–0.85 ranges are the paper's own text.
